title: Polymorphism and pattern matching
lesson:
**Polymorphism** ("many shapes") is the payoff of the last two units. You hold a `List<Enemy>`, call the same method on each, and each one does its own thing:

```
foreach (Enemy e in wave)
    log.Add(e.Act(distance));
```

A goblin runs closer, an archer shoots, a healer heals. The loop has no `if (e is Goblin)` in it, and when you add a `Bomber` next week the loop doesn't change. That's the habit to build: **put the behaviour in the class, not in a big if-chain outside it.**

**The common mistake** is the type-checking chain:

```
if (e is Goblin) ... else if (e is Archer) ... else if (e is Healer) ...
```

Every new enemy means hunting down every chain like this. If you catch yourself writing one over your own classes, an overridden method is usually the better answer.

**But sometimes you don't own the classes.** Loot on the ground might be a `Coin`, a `Potion`, a `Key` or a plain string note, with no shared base. Then C#'s **pattern matching** is the clean tool:

```
string Describe(object item) => item switch
{
    null => "Nothing",
    Coin { Value: >= 100 } c => $"Treasure! {c.Value} gold",
    Coin c => $"{c.Value} gold",
    Potion p => $"Potion (+{p.Heal} HP)",
    string note => $"Note: {note}",
    _ => "Unknown item"
};
```

- `Coin c` is a **type pattern**: "if it's a Coin, call it c".
- `{ Value: >= 100 }` is a **property pattern**: also check a property.
- Order matters: the first matching arm wins, so put the special case (big coin) **before** the general one (any coin).
- `_` is the catch-all. Without it, an unexpected item throws at runtime.

The `is` keyword does the same check inside an `if`:

```
if (item is Key k && k.Door == "crypt") ...
```

`is` both checks the type and gives you a typed variable, so you never need a risky cast like `(Key)item`, which crashes if you're wrong.

In Unity you'll use both: virtual methods for your own enemy types, and `if (other.TryGetComponent(out IDamageable d))` or `is` checks for whatever a raycast happened to hit.

notes: Each enemy class decides its own action; the loop just calls Act.
Adding a new enemy means adding a class, not editing the loop.
The switch expression checks types top to bottom; the first match wins.
`when` adds an extra condition to a pattern; `_` catches anything left.

exercises.title: Every enemy acts
exercises.prompt:
Enemy is given. Write three kinds, each with a constructor taking the name:
- Goblin: Act(distance) is "{Name} attacks" when distance <= 1, else "{Name} runs closer".
- Archer: "{Name} shoots" when distance >= 3, else "{Name} steps back".
- Healer: always "{Name} heals the wave".
Then Wave.TakeTurn(enemies, distance) returns each enemy's action in order. TakeTurn must not check types: let each class decide.

tests.call: Wave.TakeTurn(new List<Enemy> { new Goblin("Snik"), new Archer("Kip"), new Healer("Mo") }, 1)
tests.expect: [Snik attacks, Kip steps back, Mo heals the wave]
tests.name: close up

tests.call: Wave.TakeTurn(new List<Enemy> { new Goblin("Snik"), new Archer("Kip"), new Healer("Mo") }, 5)
tests.expect: [Snik runs closer, Kip shoots, Mo heals the wave]
tests.name: far away

tests.why: TakeTurn shouldn't check types: call e.Act(distance) and let each class decide.

hints: public class Goblin : Enemy { public Goblin(string name) : base(name) { } public override string Act(int distance) => ...; }
Use a ternary: distance <= 1 ? $"{Name} attacks" : $"{Name} runs closer"

exercises.title: What did I pick up?
exercises.prompt:
Coin, Potion and Key are given (they share no base class). Write Pickup.Describe(object item) with a switch expression:
- null: "Nothing"
- a Coin worth 100 or more: "Treasure! {Value} gold"
- any other Coin: "{Value} gold"
- a Potion: "Potion (+{Heal} HP)"
- a Key: "Key to the {Door}"
- a string: "Note: {text}"
- anything else: "Unknown item"

tests.expect: Key to the crypt | Note: Go north
tests.name: key and note

hints: public static string Describe(object item) => item switch { ... };
Put the special coin first: Coin { Value: >= 100 } c => $"Treasure! {c.Value} gold",

exercises.title: Counting the loot
exercises.prompt:
Using `is` patterns (no casts), write in static class Loot:
- int TotalGold(List<object> items): coins count their Value, each Potion is worth 10, everything else (keys, nulls, strings, numbers) is worth 0.
- bool CanOpen(List<object> items, string door): true if there is a Key for that door (door names match ignoring case).

tests.call: Loot.TotalGold(new List<object> { new Coin(5), new Potion(30), new Coin(20), new Key("gate") })
tests.name: coins and a potion

tests.call: Loot.CanOpen(new List<object> { new Coin(5), new Key("Gate") }, "gate").ToString()
tests.name: the key fits

tests.call: Loot.CanOpen(new List<object> { new Coin(5), new Key("crypt") }, "gate").ToString()
tests.name: wrong key
junk is ignored
tests.hint_if_fail: `is` is false for null, so null items are safe to skip.

tests.why: Use an `is` pattern: if (item is Coin c) ...

hints: foreach (object item in items) { if (item is Coin c) total += c.Value; else if (item is Potion) total += 10; }
CanOpen: if (item is Key k && string.Equals(k.Door, door, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) return true;
No casts like (Coin)item: `is` checks and names it in one go.

quiz.q: List<Enemy> holds a Goblin and an Archer. e.Act(5) on each runs…
You add a Bomber enemy. With polymorphism, what changes in Wave.TakeTurn?
quiz.why: The behaviour lives in the new class.

quiz.q: In a switch expression, Coin c is listed before Coin { Value: >= 100 }. What happens with a 500 coin?
choices: The general Coin arm wins, the treasure arm never runs
Compile always succeeds silently and both run
quiz.why: First match wins; put specific cases first (the compiler even warns).

quiz.q: Why is `item is Key k` better than `(Key)item`?
choices: It checks safely; the cast crashes if item isn't a Key

quiz.q: When is a type-pattern switch the right tool rather than a virtual method?
choices: When the types aren't yours or share no base class (loot, messages, raycast hits)
quiz.why: Own the classes: override. Don't: match.

cards.a: Same call, each object runs its own version
if (item is Coin c) total += c.Value;

cards.q: Catch-all arm in a switch expression?

explain: Explain polymorphism in your own words, with an example of a list of things that each act differently.
